newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG army chief steps down, vows to battle on.
newsitem.headline: PNG army chief steps down, vows to battle on.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's army chief, who sparked a crisis by demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan, stepped down on Tuesday but vowed to continue his political battle with the government.

Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, who turned against Chan on Monday over a plan to use foreign mercenaries to quash an island uprising, said after accepting his dismissal notice on Tuesday that the issue could not be allowed to rest.
"The issue of Sandline (a British-based mercenary outfit) is not closed, as what this government is doing I believe is wrong," Singirok said in a statement.
"It has mortgaged the country to foreigners at the expense of our four million Papua New Guineans."

Singirok said on Monday Chan would be removed from office if he refused to go, but Tuesday's statement seemed to signal that the army chief, said to be popular with his troops, was now embarking on a political campaign.
"As a citizen I call for a full inquiry into the Sandline deal. We must not let this one go," Singirok said.
The streets of Port Moresby were calm but tense as army and police force waited for the standoff to be resolved.

"I appeal to all the servicemen and their dependants to remain calm and allow justice to take its own course," Singirok said. His statement gave no details of his plans, but an aide said Singirok would explain all at a news conference on Tuesday.

Singirok brought about one of the worst crises in Papua New Guinea's 22 years of independence on Monday when he called on Chan and other ministers to resign within 48 hours or be forced out of office by his people.
Officials said on Tuesday senior PNG legal figures were meeting to discuss what charges might be brought against the 40-year-old Australian-trained soldier, who has denied mounting any sort of coup.

Singirok turned against Chan over his decision to hire foreign soldiers of fortune, mostly from Africa, to help quell a nine-year-old secessionist struggle on resource-rich Bougainville, 900 kms (560 miles) northeast of the capital.
Monday's uncertainty sent the shares of major investors in the country downwards, although PNG stocks listed on the Australian stock exchange began to recover ground on Tuesday.
Chan, who has the support of the country's powerful police force, ordered late on Monday that Singirok be replaced by little-known Colonel Alfred Aikung.
Australia, a close neighbour and the nation's biggest aid donor, on Tuesday backed Chan's decision to sack Singirok, though Canberra has opposed the use of mercenaries.

"We utterly deplore the attempts of (the) former commander-in-chief of the Papua New Guinea defence force to defy the authority of the duly elected government of Papua New Guinea," Australian Prime Minister John Howard said.

"In the circumstances, the action taken by the prime minister of Papua New Guinea, Sir Julius Chan, to remove the head of the defence force was both understandable and justifiable," he told parliament in a special announcement.
New Zealand foreign minister Don McKinnon said he hoped the crisis would now subside and all sides could go on to tackle the Bougainville conflict through negotiation.
"It's going to take a few more days and some cool heads must prevail," McKinnon told New Zealand radio.
Much of the fighting on the island has centred around the giant Panguna copper-gold mine, majority-owned by global miner RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd.

The mine closed in 1989 as the uprising began, depriving Papua New Guinea of a rich source of foreign capital. The nation relies on exports of crude oil, gold, timber, copper and coffee for its per capita gross domestic product of US$1,228.
